voiceover_script: In May 2013, a ship cook was in the bathroom at 4:30 AM when the floor flipped upside down, and his tugboat sank one hundred feet to the ocean floor. Within seconds, freezing Atlantic water swallowed the ship. Fighting through pitch blackness, Harrison Okene surfaced inside a tiny four-foot pocket of trapped air. The cold water alone should have caused hypothermia in hours. So in total darkness, he ripped down wall panels and stacked mattresses to build a tiny floating shelf above the waterline. By Hour Twenty-Four, the real killer wasn't low oxygen, it was carbon dioxide. In a sealed bubble that small, his own breath should have turned toxic. Physicists later found the twist. At one hundred feet deep, four atmospheres of pressure compressed extra oxygen into the pocket. And every splash against the water below dissolved carbon dioxide straight into the sea like a natural scrubber. At Hour Sixty, a rescue diver swam into the wreck expecting nobody alive. Suddenly, a hand reached out of the black water and grabbed his arm. Even then, he couldn't swim straight up, rising too fast would be fatal. Divers sealed him in a decompression chamber for two more days before he walked free. Sixty hours in pitch black under the sea. Honestly, how many minutes could you stay calm?
caption: In May 2013, ship cook Harrison Okene survived 60 hours trapped upside down 100 feet under the Atlantic Ocean in a 4-foot pocket of air. Honestly — how many minutes could you stay calm before panicking? #survival #truestory #ocean #deepsea #history #science #documentary
